notes: Major personal injury quantum judgment; section 117 aftercare analysis and £3.1m award are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Tinsley v Sarkar: brain injury care costs and section 117 aftercare

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Damien Tinsley suffered severe brain injury when knocked from his bicycle in May 1998; liability was compromised at 90%.
The defendant argued future care should not be awarded because Manchester Health and Social Care Trust owed section 117 aftercare after compulsory detention.
Mr Tinsley had a troubled pre-accident history of alcohol and drug misuse but had stabilised before the accident; post-injury behaviour remained highly challenging.
Experts agreed Redford Court (BIRT) could meet his needs, but the Trust was unlikely to fund that level of provision and Mr Tinsley resisted Trust assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on quantum in the High Court after compromised liability.
enrichment.outcome: Full future care and other losses were awarded; the court rejected deducting damages for possible section 117 funding and ordered £3,127,205 exclusive of interest (90% of £3,474,672).
enrichment.ratio: Section 117 aftercare is a mandatory but resource-sensitive duty distinct from National Assistance Act accommodation rights; where a tort victim is unlikely to accept or receive Trust-funded care at the level reasonably required, and there is no top-up mechanism, Hodgson v Trapp does not require the court to offset damages for a fanciful chance of public funding.
legal_issues: Whether section 117 aftercare obligations displaced the defendant's liability for private future care costs
Whether damages for care should be discounted for the chance the Trust might fund Redford Court or a cheaper placement
Appropriate care regime, multiplier and reasonable support hours for a brain-injured claimant with high-risk behaviour
Whether the claimant's preference for own accommodation should determine the care award

notes: Case stated appeal on RSPCA summons particularity; full reasoning and answers to questions.

enrichment.short_title: Nash: defective RSPCA animal cruelty summons and Crown Court appeal
key_facts: Elsie Nash was convicted of causing unnecessary suffering to 75 domestic cats at her Sutton and Erdington Cat Rescue home.
RSPCA inspectors removed 74 live cats and mummified remains of a fifth; conditions included ammonia from urine affecting cats with respiratory disease.
On Crown Court appeal, duplicity and lack of particularity in the summons were argued; prosecution confined its case to inappropriate housing conditions.
The Crown Court dismissed the appeal after finding several housing-related allegations proved; Nash received a conditional discharge limiting future cat numbers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Birmingham Crown Court to the High Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the summons was defective for lack of particularity but the defect was cured by information given before trial and appeal; Crown Court findings on proved conduct were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A Protection of Animals Act summons must identify the act or omission alleged to cause unnecessary suffering; vague wording is defective but curable if the defendant receives reasonable information to meet the case; identified conduct causing suffering to multiple animals may be charged in a single summons without duplicity per cat.
legal_issues: Whether the information afforded reasonable particulars of the charge
Whether lack of particularity rendered the information a nullity or only required further particulars
Whether Crown Court findings on ammonia and housing conditions exceeded the prosecution case after duplicity concession
Whether separate summonses were required for conduct affecting specific cats only

notes: Landmark burden-of-proof guidance in direct discrimination appeals; revised Barton guidance annexed.

enrichment.short_title: Igen v Wong: burden of proof in direct discrimination claims
key_facts: Three appeals raised interpretation of new burden-of-proof provisions in sex, race and disability discrimination legislation.
In Wong v Igen Ltd, an Afro-Caribbean employee's race discrimination claim over disciplinary proceedings succeeded before the employment tribunal.
In Emokpae v Chamberlin Solicitors, dismissal because of rumours of a relationship with a male manager was held not sex discrimination.
In Webster v Brunel University, the EAT had wrongly held the claimant need only prove the employer could have committed discriminatory acts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal appeals from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on section 63A/54A burden-of-proof provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Igen/Wong appeal dismissed; Emokpae and Webster appeals allowed with tribunal decisions set aside; revised Barton guidance approved in the annex.
enrichment.ratio: The statutory amendments shifted the evidential burden at a two-stage process: the claimant must prove facts from which the tribunal could conclude unlawful discrimination in the absence of an adequate explanation, assuming no adequate explanation at stage one; the respondent must then prove the act was not committed or was not on the prohibited ground; 'could' does not mean the claimant need only show the respondent could have committed the act.
legal_issues: Whether section 63A codified or altered pre-King v Great Britain-China Centre law on direct discrimination
Whether respondent explanations may be considered at the first stage
Construction of 'could' and whether the claimant must prove the respondent committed the discriminatory act
Appropriate comparator analysis and revision of Barton guidance paragraph 10

Barton v Investec Securities Ltd [2003] ICR 1205
Webster v Brunel University
Martin v Lancehawk Ltd
Nagarajan v London Regional Transport [2000] 1 AC 501

notes: Extensive airports White Paper judicial review; partial success on Stansted and Luton process grounds only.

enrichment.short_title: Wandsworth v SoS: judicial review of Future of Air Transport White Paper
key_facts: Local authorities and residents challenged Chapter 11 of the December 2003 White Paper on South East airport expansion.
Policies included a first new runway at Stansted around 2011-2012, endorsement of a wide-spaced Stansted runway option, and Luton runway extension support.
Claimants alleged unfair consultation, irrational commercial viability analysis and unlawful support for options not consulted upon.
The court held the overall SERAS consultation process was lawful but identified limited unfairness on Stansted runway specification and Luton extension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two linked judicial review applications challenging airport policy in the Future of Air Transport White Paper.
enrichment.outcome: Challenges succeeded only on Stansted and Luton process grounds; Heathrow and commercial viability challenges failed; relief was declaratory rather than quashing Chapter 11.
enrichment.ratio: White Paper airport policies are amenable to judicial review but political and economic planning judgments attract a heavy irrationality threshold; prescriptive endorsement of the wide-spaced Stansted runway option and implied policy support for an unconsulted Luton runway extension were procedurally unfair, though quashing the whole chapter would be disproportionate.
legal_issues: Amenability of White Paper policies to judicial review
Fairness of consultation on Stansted runway options and SERAS Stage Two
Rationality of commercial viability conclusions for a Stansted first runway
Whether Luton runway extension could receive policy support without consultation

notes: IKEA Stockport planning s.288 challenge comprehensively dismissed by Elias J.

enrichment.short_title: IKEA v SoS: challenge to refusal of Stockport out-of-town store
key_facts: IKEA sought permission for a 28,000 sq.m store on the former Thomas Storey site in Stockport after a long call-in inquiry process.

A first inspector recommended approval; the Secretary of State refused, was quashed on decision-letter errors, and after a reopened inquiry refused again following a second inspector's recommendation.
The Secretary of State found the store would draw customers beyond the Stockport sub-region, making IKEA's sequential site search inadequate.
Benefits including regeneration were outweighed by conflicts with the adopted UDP and PPG 6 sequential approach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 statutory challenge to the Secretary of State's refusal of planning permission after reopened public inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge dismissed; the Secretary of State's refusal and reasoning on catchment area, sequential analysis and development plan compliance were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Catchment area determines need and sequential analysis under PPG 6 and the McNulty statement; where a proposed store would serve a wider market than claimed, limiting the sequential search to Stockport town centre is inadequate; reasons challenges succeed only if the decision letter leaves a genuine doubt as to what was decided and why.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State adequately addressed the first inspector's report
Correct catchment area and sub-regional versus regional classification of the proposal
Adequacy of IKEA's sequential site analysis and flexibility on scale and design
Weight given to linked trips, reduced car mileage and UDP versus emerging plan policies

notes: Mannai break-clause notice appeal; Master Moncaster's decision upheld on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Peer Freeholds v Clean Wash: Mannai break notice with wrong date
key_facts: Clean Wash held a six-year lease of business premises in Thetford with a tenant break option at the end of the third year of the term (7 November 2004).
The tenant's 5 January 2004 notice stated an intention to exercise the break on 22 August 2004, coinciding with a rent review date but not the permitted break date.
The landlord declined to accept the notice as valid; the tenant vacated and litigation followed on whether the lease ended.
Master Moncaster held the notice effective despite the wrong date; the landlord appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Master Moncaster's decision refusing summary judgment and striking out the landlord's claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the break notice was valid and the lease terminated on 7 November 2004, the only date permitted by clause 6.8.
enrichment.ratio: A break notice with a wrong termination date may be valid under Mannai if a reasonable recipient with knowledge of the lease would be left in no reasonable doubt that the tenant intended to exercise the break at the permitted date; reference to 22 August explained the mistake rather than creating genuine ambiguity.
legal_issues: Construction of tenant break notice under clause 6.8 of the underlease
Application of Mannai and Garston principles to mistaken break dates
Whether a reasonable landlord could think the tenant only wanted to break on the rent review date
Objective interpretation of unilateral contractual notices
linked_authorities: Mannai Investment Co Ltd v Eagle Star Life Assurance Co Ltd [1997] AC 749
Garston v Scottish Widows Fund [1998] 1 WLR 1583
Fernandez v McDonald [2004] 1 WLR 1027

notes: Life sentence appeal; psychiatric evidence dispute resolved in favour of sentencing judge.

enrichment.short_title: R v R: life sentence rather than Hospital Order for rape
key_facts: S.R. pleaded guilty to rape of a stranger at a bus stop and attempted kidnapping of a 14-year-old girl the same day.
He used a stun gun and cosh, caused severe physical and psychological harm, and had a history of violence and schizophrenia with intermittent hospital admissions.
The sentencing judge imposed life imprisonment with a seven-year minimum term rather than a section 37/41 Hospital Order.
Psychiatrists disagreed whether paranoid schizophrenia made hospital disposal more suitable than prison.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against life sentence and minimum term by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to prefer Dr Browne's view that the appellant was faking symptoms and to impose life imprisonment for public protection.
enrichment.ratio: Where consultant psychiatrists disagree on suitability of a Hospital Order under section 37, the sentencing judge who heard oral evidence is entitled to prefer one opinion; unanimous medical opinion and bed availability in Howell do not apply; prison transfer to hospital remains available under section 48 if needed.
legal_issues: Whether a Hospital Order with restriction under sections 37 and 41 was the appropriate disposal
Whether the judge erred in preferring prosecution psychiatric evidence over treating psychiatrist Dr Sarkar
Assessment of dangerousness and risk to women following rape and attempted kidnapping
Application of R v Howell where medical opinions are not unanimous
linked_authorities: R v Howell (7 Cr App R(S) 360)

confidence.notes: Single issue appeal with clear appellate endorsement of the judge's psychiatric findings.

notes: Surrender by operation of law appeal; landlord omissions insufficient for implied surrender.

enrichment.short_title: Bellcourt v Adesina: rent arrears after alleged tenancy surrender
key_facts: Mrs Adesina took a lease of dilapidated Plumstead High Street premises in August 2000 but paid no rent and only half the deposit.
She left in November 2000 after complaining of misrepresentation; the landlord did not demand December quarter rent or seek re-entry until forfeiture in November 2001.
The trial judge held conduct of both parties showed surrender by operation of law around mid-December 2000.
The landlord appealed, arguing mere omission to demand rent could not amount to acceptance of surrender.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from county court judgment limiting rent arrears to one quarter after implied surrender.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; no surrender by operation of law was established; the landlord remained entitled to arrears accruing until forfeiture on 12 November 2001.
enrichment.ratio: Surrender by operation of law requires unequivocal conduct by both parties inconsistent with the tenancy continuing; tenant abandonment and landlord silence, including failure to demand rent, are insufficient; telling the council the tenant remained liable for rates is inconsistent with accepted surrender.
legal_issues: Whether tenant departure and landlord inaction constituted surrender by operation of law
Whether Brent v Sharma and Vyas supported implied surrender on similar facts
Onus on tenant to prove lease termination when disputing rent liability
Whether acts of omission alone can be unequivocal landlord acceptance of surrender

enrichment.short_title: OBG v Allan: costs and permission after receivers judgment
key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal's substantive judgment in OBG Ltd v Allan on receivers' liability, further issues arose as to form of order and costs.
Damages were agreed at £244,000 plus interest of £140,527.02, replacing the trial judge's higher figure.
The court ordered OBG to pay 80% of receivers' appeal and cross-appeal costs in the Court of Appeal, with costs below remitted to the trial judge.
Permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused, leaving important issues for possible further appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Post-judgment hearing in the Court of Appeal on order form, costs and permission to appeal after OBG v Allan.
enrichment.outcome: Agreed damages and interest substituted; OBG to pay 80% of appellate costs; below-trial costs remitted to the judge; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party succeeds on the bulk of appellate issues, an 80% costs order against the unsuccessful party is appropriate; costs below should reflect the court's substantive judgments and be determined by the trial judge unless agreed.
legal_issues: Form of order reflecting agreed quantum and interest after appellate decision
Apportionment of Court of Appeal costs between successful appellants and partial winners

notes: Attorney General reference; unduly lenient snooker club robbery sentences increased.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref: unduly lenient armed snooker club robbery sentences
key_facts: Three young offenders robbed a Deptford snooker club at night using a stun gun and cosh after waiting until only one staff member remained.
Victim Mr Yaldiz was repeatedly stunned, beaten and kicked; CCTV tapes were stolen; about £1,600 was taken.
Dervishi and Sejdial pleaded guilty on the day of trial; Kalemi was convicted after trial; sentences ranged from four to five-and-a-half years.
The victim suffered lasting psychological harm including depression and inability to work.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference upheld; sentences quashed and replaced with 7 years' detention for Dervishi and Sejdial and 8 years for Kalemi, reflecting double jeopardy reduction from expected post-trial levels.
enrichment.ratio: Carefully planned night-time robbery of vulnerable premises with weapons and gratuitous violence against an incapacitated victim warrants substantially higher youth custody than four to five-and-a-half years; troubled Kosovo backgrounds explain conduct but do not significantly mitigate serious joint enterprise robbery.
legal_issues: Whether four to five-and-a-half year terms were unduly lenient for armed robbery with stun gun and cosh
Appropriate starting points after late guilty pleas versus trial conviction
Weight of aggravating features including planning, weapons and psychological harm
Mitigation from age, late pleas and difficult personal histories

R v Evans [2001] 1 Cr App R(S) 454
